question: After every attention and MLP weight matrix in a pretrained LLM has been reduced to 16, 32, or 64 shared scalar K-means centroids, which properties of the fixed-assignment centroid vector—relative order, sign, scale, offset, moments, or higher-order shape—actually preserve perplexity and downstream behavior under single-layer and cumulative perturbations, and what compression and inference trade-offs result?

key_findings.claim: Aggressive scalar weight clustering preserves much, but not all, of the three tested models' language-model quality without post-clustering training.
key_findings.evidence: The method clusters Q/K/V/O and MLP gate/up/down matrices while leaving embeddings, normalization parameters, and the LM head dense. Adaptive K-means changes Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct WikiText-2 perplexity from 8.64 to 9.08 and a CompactifAI-compressed Llama 3B from 11.88 to 12.32 in the internal harness; SmolLM2-135M's fully clustered baseline is 27.52. These are useful compression baselines, but they already contain a measurable loss and K is selected per component against the same perplexity criterion.

anchors.section: II. K-means Clustering of LLM Weights

key_findings.claim: Clustering largely preserves the seven reported downstream accuracies, but the changes are mixed rather than uniformly negligible.
key_findings.evidence: From Figure 2, original Llama versus clustered Llama changes BoolQ 0.84→0.82, GSM8K 0.75→0.67, HellaSwag 0.79→0.80, Lambada OpenAI 0.73→0.69, Lambada Standard 0.66→0.62, MMLU 0.68→0.66, and TriviaQA 0.74→0.71. The compressed 3B model changes 0.83→0.81, 0.64→0.60, 0.67→0.67, 0.62→0.55, 0.54→0.49, 0.59→0.56, and 0.46→0.43, respectively. The largest displayed losses are eight points on GSM8K for 8B and seven points on Lambada OpenAI for 3B, so 'largely preserves' is defensible in aggregate but hides task-specific sensitivity.

key_findings.claim: At one representative mid-depth gate projection, preserving centroid order is much safer than breaking it, even when the replacement values are numerically far from the originals.
key_findings.evidence: In Table I at layer 10 with K=32, sorted-Gaussian rank-preserving replacement gives PPL 9.17/12.46/28.35 on Llama 8B/Compressed Llama 3B/SmolLM2 versus clustered baselines 9.08/12.32/27.52; frequency-weighted monotone replacement gives 9.17/12.48/28.28. By contrast, sign-preserving but order-breaking replacement gives 9.56/13.37/36.58, random Gaussian gives 9.76/20.98/43.92, and a full random centroid permutation gives 20.67/460.2/3,151.

key_findings.claim: Centroid order dominates centroid sign in the selected mid-layer experiment.
key_findings.evidence: The order-preserving/sign-scrambling condition stays at PPL 9.13, 12.33, and 27.53, nearly the three baselines, whereas the sign-preserving/order-breaking condition rises to 9.56, 13.37, and 36.58. This isolates order more cleanly than the Gaussian comparison, but it remains one matrix per model and one reported draw.

anchors.section: III.A.2 Scrambling Centroid Signs and Table I

key_findings.claim: The title's literal 'only relative ranks matter' is falsified by the paper's own rank-preserving transformations.
key_findings.evidence: Every Table II transform preserves centroid order, yet power compression sign(w)|w|^0.5 sends PPL from 9.08 to 1,159.52 for Llama 8B and from 12.32 to 1,510.1 for compressed Llama 3B; SmolLM2 degrades more mildly from 27.52 to 31.51. Tanh with α=3 gives 11.33/15.89/33.90, while simple scaling by two gives 9.59/13.10/30.58. Rank is therefore an important conditional invariant, not a sufficient statistic by itself; variance, depth, residual accumulation, and higher moments also matter.

anchors.section: III.A.3 Which Rank-Preserving Randomizations Are Safe?

key_findings.claim: Depth changes the tolerance to both order-preserving and order-breaking centroid perturbations by orders of magnitude.
key_findings.evidence: Table III reports, for Llama 8B, early-layer PPL 117.39 under order-preserving/sign-breaking replacement and 2,260 under random Gaussian, versus 9.13 and 9.76 at layer 10. Compressed Llama 3B reaches 78,847 for sign-preserving/order-breaking and 28,315 for random Gaussian at layer 1; SmolLM2 reaches 665,943 for sign-preserving/order-breaking at layer 28. Even monotone Gaussian replacement is not uniformly safe: it gives 102.6 at the compressed model's layer 1 and 39.40 at SmolLM2 layer 28.

anchors.section: III.A.4 Dependence of Randomization on Layer Depth and Table III

key_findings.claim: When rank-preserving replacements are accumulated from deep to shallow blocks, uncorrected scale drift rapidly destroys all three models; moment correction delays but does not prevent collapse.
key_findings.evidence: In Figure 3 the uncorrected monotone-random curves exceed 10^5 times baseline after only two blocks. With affine correction to reconstructed-weight mean and variance, Llama 8B remains within 1.6× baseline through 56% of the network, compressed Llama 3B within 2× through about 50%, and SmolLM2 is already 5× baseline at one-third and collapses around 67%. The experiment supports the narrower claim that first- and second-moment drift explains much of cumulative failure on this single replacement path; it does not establish that scale drift dominates all possible multi-layer perturbations.

anchors.section: III.B Randomizing Multiple Layers and Figure 3

key_findings.claim: The paper's affine 'safe transformation' statement is internally inconsistent if it is read as a nontrivial affine map that preserves the original mean and variance.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 2–3 require f to preserve the reconstructed distribution's mean and variance, then Equation 4 names f(w)=aw+b, a>0 as the natural choice. Applied directly to a distribution, the transformed moments are aμ+b and a²σ², so exact preservation of the same nonzero variance forces a=1 and b=0. A nontrivial monotone draw can instead be affinely normalized back to target moments, as the progressive experiment appears to do, but that is different from claiming an arbitrary affine transform itself preserves the original distribution. Table II confirms w→0.5w and w→2w change variance fourfold in opposite directions.

key_findings.claim: The proposed normalization explanation does not match the tested Llama-family architectures as written.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 5 correctly shows that an elementwise affine weight transform maps each linear output to ay_o+b∑_d x_d and preserves output-neuron order for a>0. The paper then says a subsequent LayerNorm subtracts the common offset and absorbs scale, and that monotone nonlinearities 'including SiLU' preserve order. The tested Llama and SmolLM families use RMSNorm, which rescales without subtracting the activation mean, and SiLU is not globally monotone on its negative tail. Thus the one-layer >0.99 post-normalization cosine result is empirical support for that case, but the stated mechanism is not a valid general derivation for these models.

key_findings.claim: The compact object that is kept fixed is not rank alone: the full high-dimensional cluster-label matrix retains every weight's spatial assignment.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 reconstructs each weight as c_{L[d,o]}; all randomization experiments fix L and alter only c. Consequently, successful order-preserving randomization shows that precise values within an already learned label pattern are flexible. It does not show that a weight matrix can be specified from centroid ranks alone, nor that arbitrary label assignments with the same centroid order work. The authors themselves conclude that the label structure is the primary remaining bottleneck after centroid healing.

anchors.section: II. K-means Clustering of LLM Weights, Equation 1
IV. Relation to Quantization and Codebook Methods

key_findings.claim: Centroid occupancy is sharply imbalanced, providing a plausible reason that preserving a near-zero-to-tail ladder can work.
key_findings.evidence: For a 7,168×2,816 compressed-model gate projection with 20.2 million values and K=32, 19 centroids cover 90% of weights and each of two or three near-zero centroids receives more than 1.2 million weights. The paper infers that sparse tail clusters retain extreme connections, but it does not directly identify known super weights or ablate those clusters.

anchors.section: III.C Centroids Have a Near-Normal Distribution

key_findings.claim: The disk-compression trade-off is real, but scalar clustering alone saves no accelerator memory in the supported rebuild-to-dense path.
key_findings.evidence: Table V reports dense FP16 at 15.0 GB disk, 14.96 GB GPU, PPL 8.87 and clustered-original at 6.9 GB disk, the same 14.96 GB GPU, PPL 9.32. Compressed+clustered is 3.2 GB disk, 6.01 GB GPU, PPL 13.36; adding AWQ yields 2.6 GB disk, 2.55 GB GPU, PPL 13.86. The memory gain in the last two configurations comes from structural pre-compression and INT4, because clustered weights are reconstructed to dense tensors at load time.

anchors.section: IV. Relation to Quantization and Codebook Methods
Appendix A.1 Internal Throughput and Appendix C introduction

key_findings.claim: Centroid-only fine-tuning gives a modest recovery, not a full repair of clustering loss.
key_findings.evidence: In the vLLM harness, compressed Llama has PPL 12.62, clustering raises it to 13.36, and centroid-only fine-tuning lowers it to 13.05. That recovers 0.31 of the 0.74 added-perplexity gap, or 41.9%, slightly above the prose's '30–40%' range, while remaining 0.43 worse than the unclustered compressed model. The paper gives no training corpus, optimizer, schedule, validation split, or compute accounting for this healing experiment.

anchors.section: IV. Relation to Quantization and Codebook Methods

key_findings.claim: The appendix's direct indexed lookup implementations are negative results: they erase the expected arithmetic advantage and are much slower than dense execution.
key_findings.evidence: Table VII gives 155 tok/s for original rebuild-to-dense, 157 for clustered-original rebuild, 259 for pre-compressed, 269 for pre-compressed+clustered rebuild, but only 14 for original LUT and 34 for pre-compressed LUT—roughly 11–14× lower throughput than the corresponding rebuild paths. Table VIII gives 0.65 s for dense CPU execution and 2.94–4.25 s for four LUT/gather variants, or 4.52–6.53× slower. The authors attribute the failure to row-level partitions with effective codebook size near the output dimension, little centroid reuse, irregular gathers, and cache stalls.

anchors.section: Appendix C. Inference Speed and Execution Paths
Tables VII-VIII and Appendix C.a Why LUT Execution Is Slow

key_findings.claim: Rebuild-to-dense clustering is throughput-neutral; speedups belong to the separate pre-compression stage.
key_findings.evidence: On an H200 internal harness, Table VI reports 2,194 generated tokens/s for dense FP16 and approximately 2,194 for clustered-original, versus 6,991 for pre-compressed and 6,872 for pre-compressed+clustering. The vLLM figures show the same separation. This directly limits any implication that reducing distinct scalar values accelerates inference without a specialized representation and kernel.

anchors.section: Appendix A.1 Internal Throughput and Table VI

key_findings.claim: Most components require K=32, and pre-compression increases the number of K=64 components needed to satisfy the tolerance.
key_findings.evidence: Table IX assigns the pre-compressed model 55/29 MLP and 91/21 attention projections to K=32/K=64; original Llama has 78/18 and 114/14; SmolLM2 has 1/66/23 MLP and 9/84/27 attention at K=16/32/64. Thus the pre-compressed Llama uses 50 K=64 components versus 32 for original Llama, while only SmolLM2 uses K=16 at all.

anchors.section: Appendix D. Per-Layer Cluster Budget Distribution and Table IX

key_findings.claim: Absolute perplexities in the controlled experiments and storage table cannot be compared because the paper uses two harnesses.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B states that Section III uses lm-eval-harness while Table V and Appendix C use vLLM 0.7.3 and that only within-harness comparisons are meaningful. Accordingly, the same compressed+clustered model is PPL 12.32 in Section III but 13.36 in Table V; dense/clustered Llama is 8.64/9.08 internally but 8.87/9.32 in vLLM. This is disclosed rather than a hidden discrepancy, but it prevents a single cross-table accuracy frontier.

method.core_idea: Use scalar K-means weight sharing as a controlled intervention: retain the learned label matrix that assigns every matrix entry to a cluster, alter only the K centroid values, and compare order-preserving against order-breaking reconstructions at individual depths and cumulatively through the network.
method.mechanism: For every attention Q/K/V/O and MLP gate/up/down matrix, the authors choose K∈{16,32,64} independently using a single-component WikiText-2 sensitivity limit of +0.5 PPL, run scalar K-means, store a packed label matrix L and FP16 centroids c, and reconstruct W-hat[d,o]=c[L[d,o]]. Embeddings, normalization parameters, and the LM head remain unclustered. Controlled tests keep L fixed and replace c with random Gaussian values, a permutation, sign- or order-controlled values, affine scalings, tanh transforms, or power transforms. Single-layer tests compare layer depths; a multi-layer test replaces blocks from deepest to shallowest with monotone-random centroids, with and without affine matching of reconstructed-weight mean and variance. A centroid-only healing experiment and two runtime paths—load-time dense reconstruction and direct indexed lookup—measure practical trade-offs.
assumptions: WikiText-2 perplexity is a sufficient sensitivity criterion for choosing each matrix's K and for inferring general model robustness.
A +0.5 single-component perplexity allowance is an appropriate and comparable budget across architectures, layers, and baseline perplexities.

Holding the entire label matrix L fixed isolates the causal contribution of centroid values without making the headline 'ranks alone' misleading; in fact, L retains the matrix's high-dimensional spatial structure.
One random replacement per condition is representative despite stochastic K-means initialization and stochastic centroid draws.
A one-matrix intervention at the selected layer 10 gate projection generalizes to other matrices before the depth sweep samples only a few of them.
Perplexity is an adequate proxy for downstream capability under the perturbations; downstream tasks are evaluated for clustering but not for the rank interventions themselves.
Centroid ranks are well-defined and ties induced by finite precision do not materially alter the argument.
Mean and variance of a whole reconstructed matrix are the relevant scale statistics, even though per-channel and activation-conditioned moments may be more consequential.
Layer normalization approximately absorbs a common output offset and scale; the argument is presented for mean-subtracting LayerNorm although the tested Llama-family models use RMSNorm.
SiLU behaves monotonically for the activation regime that matters, although it is not globally monotone.
Deep-to-shallow block replacement is representative of cumulative perturbation orders and interactions.
The private CompactifAI-compressed 3B checkpoint and undocumented centroid-healing run are comparable and reproducible enough to support the reported generalization.
Disk compression from packed labels can be separated from runtime memory and speed; deployability requires rebuilding dense weights unless a structured/fused lookup kernel is available.
Observed robustness across one Llama 8B, one derived Llama 3B, and SmolLM2-135M transfers to other model families, sizes, modalities, and normalization designs.

techniques.role: Applies scalar K-means to each attention and MLP weight matrix and selects 16, 32, or 64 centroids under a per-component perplexity budget.
Separates the fixed cluster-label matrix L from the centroid vector c so value structure can be perturbed without changing weight locations.
Contrasts sorted or frequency-weighted random centroids with unsorted Gaussian values and centroid permutations.
Compares order-preserving/sign-breaking and sign-preserving/order-breaking replacements to separate sign from global order.
Applies affine, tanh, and signed-power maps that retain rank while changing scale, tails, and higher moments.
Repeats centroid interventions at selected early, middle, late, and attention projections in each model.
Perturbs blocks from deepest to shallowest to expose compounding errors across network depth.
Matches reconstructed-weight mean and variance after monotone randomization to test whether cumulative collapse is driven by scale drift.
Fine-tunes shared centroid values while preserving label assignments to recover part of the clustering-induced accuracy gap.
Stores cluster identifiers in ceil(log2 K) bits plus a short FP16 codebook and optionally entropy-compresses labels for disk reduction.
Benchmarks dense load-time reconstruction against direct label/centroid lookup on GPU serving and several CPU implementations.

limitations: Author-stated: rank preservation is not sufficient in early layers, under extreme nonlinear transformations, or when perturbations accumulate across many layers; scale, offset, and higher-order shape also matter.

Author-stated: direct indexed LUT execution is currently 11–14× slower than rebuild-to-dense GPU execution and 4.5–6.5× slower than dense CPU execution because plain scalar labels provide little reuse and irregular access dominates.
Author-stated: without specialized kernels, clustering reduces storage on disk but reconstructs dense weights at load time and therefore does not reduce runtime GPU memory.
Author-stated: absolute perplexities from the internal lm-eval stack and vLLM 0.7.3 are not comparable; only within-harness differences are meaningful.
Author-stated: the paper does not propose a new compression method; it uses established scalar K-means weight sharing as a probe of weight structure.
Author-stated: future work is needed to characterize safe simultaneous transformations, differentiably optimize assignments, and bound when centroid rank is an approximate sufficient statistic.

Reviewer-inferred: the literal title and repeated broad phrasing overclaim the results. The fixed label matrix, moments, higher-order shape, layer depth, normalization, residual path, and transformation extent all matter, and a rank-preserving map produces PPL above 1,000 in two models.

Reviewer-inferred: the controlled rank experiments report no seeds, repeated K-means runs, repeated centroid draws, confidence intervals, or error bars; a stochastic contrast may depend on an unreported realization.
Reviewer-inferred: K is chosen per component using up to +0.5 WikiText-2 PPL and then evaluated primarily on WikiText-2, creating tuning/selection dependence; no held-out corpus selects K.

Reviewer-inferred: the main intervention preserves L, a full matrix of cluster identities. It identifies flexibility of representative values conditional on learned spatial assignments, not sufficiency of an ordered K-vector for model behavior.

Reviewer-inferred: downstream tasks are shown only before and after clustering. The central rank, sign, scale, and cumulative-randomization claims are supported solely by perplexity, so capability-specific consequences remain untested.

Reviewer-inferred: model breadth is limited to one public Llama 8B instruction model, one private derived Llama 3B checkpoint, and one 135M Smol model; there are no base models, MoEs, encoder models, non-language networks, or alternative normalization families.
Reviewer-inferred: the affine/LayerNorm explanation is mismatched to RMSNorm-based tested architectures, and SiLU is incorrectly described as monotone without restricting its input range.

Reviewer-inferred: exact mean-and-variance preservation by a nontrivial affine self-map is mathematically impossible for a nondegenerate distribution; the prose conflates applying an affine map with using an affine normalization after a random monotone draw.

Internal-contradiction audit (reviewer-identified): page 5 says the same affine map is applied to 'all layers simultaneously' and cites Table II as global evidence, but Table II's caption restricts every transform to layers.10.mlp.gate_proj; the release gives no separate all-layer affine-scaling result beyond the different progressive monotone-random experiment in Figure 3.

Reviewer-inferred: centroid healing is insufficiently specified—training data, objective, optimizer, learning rate, steps, compute, held-out selection, and variance are absent—so its claimed minimal cost and reproducibility cannot be assessed.
Reviewer-inferred: the compressed 3B model is not a public, independently specified baseline, and its prior structural compression may entangle sensitivity with the clustering intervention.
Reviewer-inferred: there is no end-to-end wall-clock cost for K-means fitting, adaptive K search, label entropy coding, dense reconstruction at startup, or centroid healing.

Reviewer-inferred: the claimed absence of a post-hoc remedy for scrambled ranks is an absence-of-evidence statement; no repair algorithm is attempted, and the original order is trivially recoverable if its permutation is retained.
failure_modes: Author-demonstrated: a full centroid permutation at a single mid-layer gate sends PPL to 20.67, 460.2, and 3,151 across the three models.
Author-demonstrated: order-preserving signed-power γ=0.5 still sends Llama 8B and compressed Llama 3B to PPL 1,159.52 and 1,510.1, falsifying unqualified rank sufficiency.

Author-demonstrated: early or architecture-specific sensitive layers can fail under monotone replacements; compressed Llama layer 1 reaches 102.6 under monotone Gaussian replacement, and SmolLM2 layer 28 reaches 39.40.

Author-demonstrated: uncorrected progressive rank-preserving replacement collapses above 10^5× baseline after only two blocks; even moment-corrected SmolLM2 collapses around two-thirds of the network.
Author-demonstrated: direct indexed execution is kernel-bound and can turn an apparent O(DK+KO) arithmetic reduction into an 11–14× GPU throughput loss or 4.5–6.5× CPU slowdown.

Reviewer-inferred: a centroid map can preserve global rank and moments yet damage per-channel scales, activation-conditioned statistics, skew, kurtosis, or tails, producing failures that the global correction cannot anticipate.
Reviewer-inferred: RMSNorm does not remove a common additive activation offset, so transformations with b≠0 can accumulate differently from the paper's LayerNorm argument.
Reviewer-inferred: negative-tail SiLU inputs can reverse local ordering because SiLU is not globally monotone, breaking the proposed order-propagation chain.
Reviewer-inferred: the adaptive +0.5 PPL rule can spend the tolerance repeatedly across matrices; individually acceptable clusterings may interact badly when applied jointly.
Reviewer-inferred: packed random-looking label matrices compress on disk but exhibit insufficient local reuse for fast lookup, forcing a choice between compact residency and performant dense GEMM.

Reviewer-inferred: rare function-critical weights may be averaged into tail clusters unless K-means isolates them; the superweight explanation is conjectural because no coordinate-level preservation test is performed.
Reviewer-inferred: conclusions may reverse under a different random draw or K-means initialization because all reported contrasts appear to lack repetitions and uncertainty estimates.
reusable_insights: Factor a compressed weight matrix into discrete assignments and representative values, then intervene on only one factor; this yields a much cleaner structural test than perturbing quantized weights wholesale.
A useful ablation crosses sign preservation with order preservation. It can show that a global ordering ladder, rather than zero-crossing alone, carries model information.
Any claim that an invariant is sufficient should include adversarial transformations that preserve that invariant. The signed-power γ=0.5 case is an unusually informative negative control.
Test perturbations at early, middle, and late depths: residual accumulation can convert a benign local symmetry into catastrophic network-level drift.

Separate rank distortion from moment drift by matching reconstructed-weight statistics after a random monotone replacement, while recognizing that global first and second moments do not fix channelwise or higher-order structure.
Report storage, resident memory, load-time reconstruction, and inference throughput separately. A compact file format can offer neither memory nor speed advantages at execution time.
For lookup-based acceleration, codebook reuse and label regularity are systems prerequisites; reducing the number of unique scalar values is not enough.
Report harness boundaries explicitly. The paper's disclosure that 12.32 and 13.36 are different-stack measurements prevents a misleading cross-table comparison.
A centroid-only repair pass is a parameter-efficient diagnostic: recovery quantifies how much loss lies in representative values versus fixed assignments.
When an argument invokes normalization, derive it for the model's actual operator—RMSNorm versus LayerNorm—and audit every claimed monotonic nonlinearity over its true domain.
open_questions: Does the order-versus-sign contrast reproduce over many K-means seeds, centroid draws, corpora, and checkpoints with confidence intervals?
Which statistic predicts safety best: global centroid rank, rank within each row/channel, activation-weighted rank, cluster occupancy rank, or output-feature rank?
How much of performance is retained if the label matrix L is perturbed while centroid ranks are fixed, and which spatial structures in L are indispensable?
Can rank-preserving replacements be chosen to match per-channel means, RMS values, covariances, skewness, and kurtosis, and does that remove the remaining cumulative collapse?
What is the correct theory for affine weight changes through RMSNorm, residual addition, RoPE, gated products, and nonmonotone SiLU?
Do rank perturbations preserve downstream task accuracy, calibration, safety behavior, and generation quality as reliably as WikiText-2 perplexity?
Are super weights individually isolated by K-means tail clusters, and does preserving their magnitudes or assignments explain the model/depth outliers?
Would randomizing blocks in shallow-to-deep, interleaved, or sensitivity-ranked order yield the same scale-drift conclusion as the single deep-to-shallow path?
Can a structured label-learning objective produce enough tile-level centroid reuse for fused LUT execution to beat dense GEMM without losing accuracy?
How do adaptive K selection and cluster occupancy behave on MoEs, larger models, base checkpoints, multilingual models, and non-RMSNorm architectures?
What exact data, compute, and optimization schedule makes centroid-only healing effective, and does a held-out evaluation confirm the 41.9% recovery?
Can rank scrambling actually be repaired by relearning only centroids, a permutation, normalization parameters, or low-rank adapters, contrary to the paper's 'uncorrectable' phrasing?

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Compression: Compressing Deep Neural Networks with Pruning, Trained Quantization and Huffman Coding
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational direct predecessor for K-means weight sharing, centroid retraining, and entropy coding.
competitive_landscape.difference: Han, Mao, and Dally already cluster trained weights into shared values, fine-tune the shared centroids, and Huffman-code weights/indices. The target transfers scalar clustering to LLM matrices and contributes controlled rank/sign/scale interventions plus modern serving measurements; neither basic K-means weight sharing, packed labels, centroid healing, nor entropy-coded storage is new here.

competitive_landscape.title: eDKM: An Efficient and Accurate Train-time Weight Clustering for Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: eDKM incorporates differentiable K-means during LLM fine-tuning, jointly adapting assignments and representatives, and reports a LLaMA-7B 3-bit reduction from 12.6 GB to 2.5 GB plus decoder-memory and task results. The target instead performs post-training clustering and freezes assignments to study centroid invariants; its interpretive intervention is distinct, while its practical clustering/healing pipeline is less optimized and not a new compression method.

competitive_landscape.title: Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Strong learned-codebook compression baseline explicitly compared by the target.
competitive_landscape.difference: AQLM uses multiple additive vector codebooks and optimizes assignments for sub-3-bit LLM compression, with dedicated inference paths; it targets the accuracy/compression frontier rather than scalar-centroid interpretability. The target's clean separation of one scalar label matrix and ordered centroids enables rank interventions, but its disk compression and runtime performance are not competitive evidence of a new method.
competitive_landscape.source_version: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research volume 235, ICML 2024, pages 12284-12303

competitive_landscape.title: SKIM: Any-bit Quantization Pushing The Limits of Post-Training Quantization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest omitted post-training scaled-K-means LLM quantization competitor.
competitive_landscape.difference: SKIM combines scaled K-means, trainable per-channel scaling, greedy mixed-precision allocation, and any-bit PTQ, reporting about 14% average perplexity-gap narrowing. It directly addresses two weaknesses exposed in the target—scale sensitivity and adaptive bit allocation—before the target's submission. The target differs by holding assignments fixed and testing centroid order causally, but should not imply that adaptive K-means LLM PTQ or learned scale correction is novel.
competitive_landscape.source_version: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research volume 267, ICML 2025, pages 2520-2534

competitive_landscape.title: LCD: Advancing Extreme Low-Bit Clustering for Large Language Models via Knowledge Distillation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior low-bit LLM clustering and LUT inference competitor cited by the target.
competitive_landscape.difference: LCD learns clustering-based quantization in a knowledge-distillation framework, smooths activations, targets 2-3 bits, and reports a purpose-built LUT design with up to 6.2× inference speedup. The target uses simpler post-training scalar clusters to isolate order and candidly reports that its unstructured LUT paths are slower; its novelty is the structural probe, not low-bit clustering or accelerated lookup.

competitive_landscape.title: The Super Weight in Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest contrary evidence about exact high-leverage weight magnitudes and locations.
competitive_landscape.difference: Yu et al. show that pruning one identified parameter can raise perplexity by three orders of magnitude and that preserving super weights/activations materially improves quantization. The target conjectures that K-means tail clusters preserve such weights because of their rank, but never locates, perturbs, or magnitude-randomizes known super weights. The two views may be compatible, yet the target does not experimentally establish that rank rather than exceptional value/location explains super-weight effects.

competitive_landscape.title: CodeQuant: Unified Clustering and Quantization for Enhanced Outlier Smoothing in Low-Precision Mixture-of-Experts
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later 2026 clustering/centroid competitor found in the current search, not prior-art preemption.
competitive_landscape.difference: CodeQuant, submitted after the target and revised in August 2026, jointly uses learnable rotation to smooth activation outliers, fine-tuned weight-cluster centroids, and custom GPU/CPU kernels for MoE low-precision inference, reporting up to 4.15× speedup. It addresses the target's unstructured-label and outlier limitations but does not test rank sufficiency; because it postdates the target, it contextualizes the current frontier rather than narrowing the target's original March 2026 contribution.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors explicitly disclaim a new compression method and instead claim a new rank-based perspective: when scalar-cluster assignments are fixed, relative centroid order matters much more than exact values or signs, affine/order-preserving changes form an approximately safe class, cumulative collapse is dominated by correctable scale drift, and rank distortion has no known repair.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper contributes a clear controlled factorization of labels and centroids; sign/order ablations; monotone-transform stress tests; depth and cumulative sweeps on three clustered models; disk, memory, fine-tuning, and appendix runtime measurements. The strongest evidence is the repeated separation between order-breaking and order-preserving perturbations at matched layers. Its own negative controls sharply bound the claim: order-preserving power transforms can exceed PPL 1,000, early and late layers can be fragile, uncorrected cumulative replacements collapse immediately, and moment correction only delays failure.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is an empirical intervention framework showing that centroid ordering is a high-leverage invariant conditional on a fixed learned label matrix, moderate distributional distortion, selected layers, and limited perturbation extent. Scalar K-means weight sharing, centroid fine-tuning, packed indices, entropy coding, adaptive clustering, learned scale correction, and LUT execution all have close predecessors. The title is materially broader than the evidence: ranks are neither the only retained information nor sufficient for performance, the affine theory is internally muddled and architecturally mismatched, and 'uncorrectable' is untested. Current August 2026 work such as CodeQuant moves the engineering frontier with smoothing and kernels but postdates the target; withdrawn PolarQuant was found in the 2026 search and excluded from competitors because its current arXiv record says the author found errors.
